paragraphs.heading: Hot springs on the seabed
paragraphs.text: A hydrothermal vent is a crack in the seabed that releases water heated inside the Earth. Vents exist because the planet is geologically active and holds large amounts of water on its surface and in its crust. They are common near volcanic areas, ocean basins and hotspots, and along mid-ocean ridges, the East Pacific Rise and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge among them. Those ridges are places where two tectonic plates move apart and new crust forms.

paragraphs.heading: Very hot water
paragraphs.text: Most vent water is seawater drawn into the system near the volcano through faults, porous sediment or volcanic rock, plus some water released by rising magma. The deep water around a vent is about 2 °C, yet water leaves vents at anywhere from 60 °C up to 464 °C. Because of the high pressure at these depths, water this hot can stay liquid or become a supercritical fluid, with properties between those of a gas and a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Supercritical venting
paragraphs.text: Pure water has a critical point of 375 °C at 218 atmospheres, and a fluid vented above its critical point is supercritical. Adding salt raises that point: for seawater it is 407 °C and 298.5 bars, matching a depth of about 2,960 m. Beebe, in the Cayman Trough, is the deepest known vent site at about 5,000 m, and it has vented supercritical fluid steadily at 401 °C. Nobody yet knows whether supercritical venting matters for water circulation, mineral deposits, chemical flows or living things.

paragraphs.heading: Chimneys that grow
paragraphs.text: Some vents build roughly cylindrical chimneys. When the superheated vent water meets near-freezing seawater, minerals dissolved in it come out as particles that add to the stack. A chimney begins with the mineral anhydrite, and then sulfides of copper, iron and zinc fill its gaps, making it less porous over time. Growth of about 30 cm a day has been recorded, and some chimneys reach 60 m. One off Oregon, called Godzilla, rose to 40 m before it fell over in 1996.

paragraphs.heading: Black smokers
paragraphs.text: One kind of vent is the black smoker, a black chimney that gives off a cloud of black material. Its particles are rich in sulfur-bearing minerals called sulfides. Black smokers are most common at depths of 2,500 to 3,000 m, but they also occur shallower and deeper. Black and white smokers carry a wide range of elements into the oceans, adding to the chemistry of the global sea.

paragraphs.heading: Life around vents
paragraphs.text: Compared with most of the deep sea, vent areas are more productive, often hosting complex communities fueled by chemicals dissolved in the vent water. Chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea there form the base of the food chain, supporting giant tube worms, clams, limpets and shrimp. Vents have also been proposed as a major factor in how life first began and in how early life survived. Their conditions have been shown to support making molecules important to life.

paragraphs.heading: Vents on other worlds
paragraphs.text: Some evidence suggests that alkaline vents, or vents holding supercritical CO₂, are better at forming these organic molecules. Scientists think active vents exist on Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and on Enceladus, a moon of Saturn. Some scientists speculate that Mars once had vents too, long ago.
